title: Firefox Can Now Block Ads on iOS (but You Have to Enable It)
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 18, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Kenneth Cheung / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device, as Mozilla is slowly rolling out native ad blocking.
                                            Most ads will be blocked, but users will still see search engine ads and sponsored content from Firefox.
                                            The feature will be off by default and is not yet available to all users.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device. Mozilla is slowly rolling out native ad blocking, which you can enable once the tool is available on your account. According to Mozilla's support page detailing the new feature, Firefox will block third-party ad networks and exchanges along with many third-party ads served on websites at the network level. It will also block ad-related trackers, pop-ups, and overlays. The platform is still letting some ads through, though: For example, you'll still see ads in search results from engines like Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo, as well as sponsored content on the Firefox Home and New Tab pages. There may also be ads that aren't covered by the EasyList filter list. Of course, Firefox isn't the only browser to natively block ads on iOS. For example, both DuckDuckGo and Brave have built-in ad blocking in their mobile apps and also allow you to disable their own search ads. Note that ad-blocking functionality doesn't extend outside of the Firefox iOS app, but URL filters in iOS 26, along with a third-party app like Wipr 2, can block ads in other apps. 
Ad blocking in Firefox will be off by default. To enable it, open the iOS app, tap the three dots, and go to Settings > Browsing. Under the Content header, toggle on Ad Blocker. You can do this from the Site menu by tapping Ad Blocker (underneath the site name and URL), which will open the Browsing menu directly. The site menu will show you at a glance whether ad blocking is on or off. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Firefox says this feature is currently "experimental," meaning it hasn't yet been made available to all users, so you may not see these options in your browser settings.

title: Hundreds of Fake VPNs Are Flooding the Chrome Web Store
description:
Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Con
body:
Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        I often tell people to think of VPNs like kitchen funnels. Instead of pouring your network traffic directly into the web and spilling your metadata everywhere, you push it down a narrow tube of encryption. You point your connection exactly where it needs to go without leaking all over the place. Of course, the assumption in such an arrangement is that you trust your VPN, which controls the flow of traffic from your device to the web. But if the VPN itself is a honeypot for attackers to pry away your data, you’ve just traded several possible security risks for one guaranteed security breach. According to the team at Socket, that’s what’s been happening with over seven hundred fake VPN apps listed on the Chrome Web Store. Many of these extensions are free, some are paid, and some even pretend to be from trusted cybersecurity providers to lure users into handing over unrestricted access to their network and browser. This weekend, I dug through Socket’s report to find out exactly what was going on with these apps and how they managed to clear Web Store moderation without getting flagged by Google. I’ll share what I found and offer some tips to help you avoid these fake VPNs. What Socket found when it analyzed hundreds of suspicious Chrome extensionsIn short, Socket’s threat research team analyzed 737 suspicious Chrome extensions that claim to offer VPN and SOCKS5 proxy servers to protect your online privacy. They uncovered paid apps selling access to VPN servers that do not exist, extensions that hijack your proxy to track online activity, and several attempts to impersonate trusted VPN service providers like NordVPN and Surfshark.
Socket is a cybersecurity platform with its own GitHub extension, firewall, and CLI to help developers analyze AI-written code for malicious behavior. When they looked into these Chrome extensions, they found that they were all published by a total of 40 developer accounts and had racked up 75,486 installs from users on the Chrome Web Store. Of the 737 suspicious extensions they analyzed, Socket’s team performed a detailed analysis of the code in 525 of them. In total, these extensions amounted to 58,318 active Chrome installs at the time. As for the other 212, they were already taken off the Web Store before Socket could take a look at them. But the researchers found a number of issues right away in the extensions they did analyze, including: 274 out of 525 extensions plagiarised the branding and logo of one among 66 reputed VPN platforms, including Proton VPN, Surfshark, NordVPN, ExpressVPN, CyberGhost, and TunnelBear. Two extensions specifically impersonated AmneziaVPN and AntiZapret, which are often used to get around internet censorship and surveillance. Each extension pointed to a fixed SOCKS5 proxy without split tunneling or per-site controls, meaning that all your online activity would get routed through the same server once the extension was installed. 104 extensions using documented DNS-over-HTTPS evasion techniques to get around Chrome’s blocklists by spoofing their DNS record. Many of these VPNs advertise a paid tier with private VPN servers in Japan, Singapore, Canada, Australia, and Turkey. But these servers do not exist, because their hostnames did not resolve when Socket ran a DNS lookup against them. With the premium VPN subscriptions, there was no license verification happening internally to detect if the user had actually paid for a subscription. This is not normal for any web-based app or platform that offers a paid tier. One of these extensions, Burёnka VPN, does not route traffic through any servers at all. It’s just a fake UI pretending to be a real app. Another extension contains a file with a plaintext comment that simply reads, “If Chrome Web Store rejects this because of automatically opening links, we can replace it with a notification offering to go to the Telegram bot.” This shows that the developers know that their app violates Web Store policy, but intend to evade reviews instead of fixing the issue. How fake VPNs got past Chrome’s review processI’ve repeatedly found that the best laid cyber attacks aren’t necessarily the most sophisticated. Just so, none of these extensions are particularly difficult to flag in a thorough code review. They got past Chrome’s defenses because they spent a lot of time studying Web Store review processes, possibly learning to evade rejections through repeated trial and error. Many of these developers have already had their other extensions removed by Chrome following a similar report from Palo Alto Networks in June, but they immediately went on to publish new extensions using the same playbook. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Even on the occasion that a developer’s account gets pulled from the store, opening a new developer account on the Chrome Web Store costs $5. Between the 40 developer accounts mentioned in the report, it barely cost $200 to publish over 700 fake extensions that reached an audience of tens of thousands.It also helped that most of these VPNs were angled toward Russian citizens trying to bypass regional censorship regulations, so any resulting incidents would not have been widely reported outside that specific target demographic. Perhaps even more unsettlingly, in the few occasions that store moderators did flag an extension for further review, they all shared exactly identical “privacy justifications” that were little more than false reassurances to get their extensions back up.It’s easy to dismiss these fake VPNs as a regional threat aimed at Russian internet users only, but you’d be wrong. Chrome’s Web Store policies paint a troubling pattern of lax security reviews, and the same fake VPN playbook could be adapted to target citizens in the U.S., UK, EU, or anywhere else in the world. In fact, Google itself issued a critical warning in 2025, speaking of similar fake VPN activity on the Play Store for Android users. How to spot a fake VPN browser extensionSince you can’t rely on app store review processes alone, you need some way to spot fake extensions before they embed spyware into your browser. You can’t be expected to reverse engineer every extension’s manifest files like Socket did, but thankfully, you don’t have to because there are easier ways to tell if something might be amiss. Install extensions by following a link directly from the VPN provider’s official website, not the search bar on Web Store or Google Play. Always read reviews before installing a new browser extension. If too many people are complaining about security concerns, avoid it.Before you install a Chrome Web Store extension, look past the app listing and user reviews to the developer account tied to that app as well. Check if the account is officially associated with the VPN provider and see if Web Store reviews flag security concerns on their other apps too. Use a tool like WhatIsMyIPAddress.com to check your currently visible IP address. Confirm that it matches the IP address displayed in your VPN extension’s UI. Run a DNS leak check while your VPN is on to make sure that it’s working properly, not merely concealing your IP address but also encrypting your DNS queries. If either your IP address, general location, or internet service provider (ISP) shows up in the test results, that’s a red flag.

title: Why Everyday Athletes Are Testing Their Sweat (and Why It's MostlyPointless)
body:
Meredith Dietz
                            
        
            Meredith Dietz
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceMeredith is a marathon runner and stand-up comedian. As Lifehacker’s Senior Staff Writer, she covers personal fitness tech, home gym equipment, and more.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 20, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Adobe Stock
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        TrainingPeaks—the training-log app plenty of serious runners, cyclists, and triathletes live in—recently rolled out a direct integration with hDrop, a reusable wearable sweat sensor. The idea is that athletes wear it on their arm, and sweat loss and sodium loss data get logged alongside their workout notes, right next to heart rate and power. The integration lets hDrop users sync hydration metrics like sweat loss, sodium loss, and hydration behavior directly into TrainingPeaks, becoming part of the same decision-making metrics as heart rate or pace.At charging $249.99 for its wearable hydration sensor, hDrop isn't alone. Two other big names in wearable sweat sensors are Nix (around $189) and FlowBio (around $340). On the budget end, Gatorade sells single-use sweat tests for around $25. The goal of all these sweat testing wearables is to tell you exactly how much fluid and sodium you're losing on a run or ride.As a marathon runner myself, it's easy to see the appeal of these products. After all, in an actual lab, sweat testing can be used to guide personalized fluid and electrolyte replacement recommendations for serious athletes. These consumer sweat sensors are chasing the same promise, just without the lab settings. Unfortunately, as multiple studies have pointed out, it's tough to achieve lab-level accuracy out in the field. Let's take a look at why you most likely do not need to waste your time and money on another wearable just for sweat.
How accurate are sweat testing wearables?Researchers note that most sweat-sensing devices haven't been rigorously tested in the messy, high-heat, high-humidity conditions athletes actually train in, and that few devices have accuracy data from large field studies rather than controlled labs. A 2026 study testing sweat sodium composition and sweat loss estimation through wearable sensors concluded that measurements from these consumer devices "should currently be interpreted with caution and not considered equivalent to laboratory-grade analyses."For our purposes here, as a curious runner or cyclist, the major hurdle for consumer-level sweat tests is that your sweat is a moving target. Your sweat sodium concentration changes from one day to the next with heat acclimation, fitness, and diet. You also have to consider the one small patch of skin being sampled. A patch on your forearm or upper arm doesn't factor in the sweat coming off your back, scalp, or torso, all of which behave differently. Trying to extrapolate one patch's reading into a whole-body sweat or sodium loss number introduces a lot of room for error. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Even hDrop, Nix, and FlowBio—which all claim to be the most accurate sweat sensors on the market—have to include in their troubleshooting guidance that poor skin contact produces bad readings, as does interference from water or any other fluid but sweat. Ultimately, these devices are sensitive to moisture, temperature, and positioning—in other words, all obstacles sure to come up during the exact sweaty workout you'd want to be testing in the first place.What this means for youDon't get me wrong—I'm all for proper sweat testing if the opportunity to get into a lab comes up. In the meantime, I'd opt for free, generic hydration tracking over a new wearable. Even if it's not lab-perfect, tracking your hydration can still surface useful patterns. Maybe you sweat noticeably more in humidity, or you're consistently a "salty sweater," or your losses spike late in long efforts. Logging all of that in an app like TrainingPeaks can help you spot patterns and adjust your hydration and fueling strategy from there.But the leap people make—from "my patch says I lost 900mg of sodium" to treating that as an actionable, precise number the way you'd treat heart rate or pace—isn't supported by the current accuracy of consumer sweat tech. These devices are not yet a substitute for a real lab sweat test. If you're interested in finding out for yourself, go crazy. Personally, I'd rather save the money on hydration testing and instead spend it on the hydration and fueling itself.

title: Google Will Soon Let You Tell It What Stories You Want to See in Your Discovery Feed
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: John Lamb via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google will soon let you tell its app what stories you want to see in your Discovery feed, adding another natual language prompt to the experience.
                                            Once the feature rolls out, you can tap the three-dot menu on any story to tell Gemini what topics you're looking for, and continue refining as you wish.
                                            In addition, you can customize your audio briefings in Google News, and you'll likely see Google's "Add as preferred source" button on more websites.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        I don't know what the far future of tech looks like, but I know what's in store for the near future: AI. Specifically, AI that responds to natural language prompts. It's already the reality for many platforms, apps, and services: Rather than doing things yourself, you tell the AI what you want done, and it follows suit. Natural language commands are popping up everywhere, from coding platforms to playlist generators. Now, apparently, they're coming to your news app too. Natural language commands are coming to the Google app's Discovery feed
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
Google announced a handful of changes coming to its self-named app on Friday. Perhaps most notably among the developments is the new ability to "tune" and "tailor" your Discovery feed to your liking—not by giving feedback for specific articles or sources, but by simply telling Google what news you want to see, and what you don't. Here's how it works, according to Google: Once the feature is live in your Google app, you can tap any three-dot menu in the feed to tell Google how you want to change your feed. When you do, you'll pull up a new window that reads "What do you want to see." Here, you'll find sample prompts ("Show me content from...," I want videos about..." etc.) and a text field to enter them in. As an example, Google says you can enter a query like "show me kitchen renovation tips and ideas." Gemini will then show you a list of the types of stories it thinks you'll want to see (e.g., "Modern layout ideas and floor plans," "Budget-friendly cabinet and countertop refreshes," etc.). If that looks good, you can hit "Refresh your feed."
If you aren't happy with Gemini's first interpretation of your instruction, you can refine it before refreshing your feed. You can send another prompt (e.g., "can you focus on eco-friendly and sustainable upgrades?") and see how Gemini responds. You can repeat this process until you're happy with the direction Gemini is taking, then hit "Refresh your feed" to see what it came up with. (Of course, you can tap a three-dot menu again to continue changing the experience.) Google says these updates will roll out "in the coming days."
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Other changes coming to the Google appIn addition to this natural language feature, Google also announced two new changes for its app. First, Google is making it easier to customize the audio briefings you might receive in Google News on Android. Now, you'll be able to choose specific topics you want to hear, including between main topics and subtopics. For example, you could say you want to hear science and technology news, but only about neuroscience and space, not environment, gaming, or virtual reality. There are a lot of curation possibilities here. In addition, Google says it's rolling out a new "Preferred Sources" button for publishers to use. You may have seen the first iteration of this button on Lifehacker articles. While it isn't clear what's new with the latest version, this button lets you tell Google that you want to see more articles from a particular publisher for topics going forward. If you add Lifehacker as a preferred source, for example, you may see our articles for topics like AI, Apple, and security when they appear in your feed.

title: What Garmin's 'Recovery Time' Estimate Actually Means
body:
Beth Skwarecki
                            
        
            Beth Skwarecki
                
                                            Senior Health Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceBeth Skwarecki is Lifehacker’s Senior Health Editor, and holds certifications as a personal trainer and weightlifting coach. She has been writing about health for over 10 years.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 20, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Beth Skwarecki
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Garmin's fitness watches often give you a "recovery time" after a workout. For example, after one easy run, it told me that I need 21 hours before I'll fully recover. I've come to expect long recovery estimates from Garmin, but they don't mean what you might think. For example, you're not expected to fully rest during that recovery time. Here's what you need to know. What is Garmin's recovery time feature, and where can you see it? You’ll see your recovery time in the end-of-workout summary that you get right after you finish a workout on many Garmin watches. It’s also available from the Training Status glance on your watch, or the Training Readiness tile in the Garmin Connect app if you have that. On my Forerunner 570, I can even set it as one of the little complications on my main watch face. The recovery time feature is available on most Enduro, Epix, Fenix, Forerunner, Instinct, Venu, and Vivoactive watches, among others (Garmin has a full list here). Garmin defines recovery time as “an estimate on how long it will take for you to fully recover and be ready for your next workout of the same intensity.” Note that phrase, fully recover. No athlete is fully recovered at the start of every training session; it's normal to carry a little fatigue from one session to the next. This number is just giving you a sense of how long you’ll be feeling the effects of this workout. 
Do you have to wait until the recovery time hits zero before working out again? No! This is probably the biggest misconception about the feature (and it explains why the recovery times can be so long—up to four days). The idea isn’t that you have to rot in bed until the timer is up. It’s just that between now and when the timer hits zero, you’ll be operating with at least a little more fatigue than usual. You can read Garmin’s explanation here. They say: “When your timer hits zero, it means you are ready to gain the maximum benefit from your next hard fitness-improving (i.e., training effect: 3.0+) type workout.”So if I get a 38-hour recovery time after a hard workout, that’s just a signal that I won’t be in tip-top shape tomorrow. If I were planning the hardest workout of my week for tomorrow, I might want to consider delaying that workout so I can do it later on fresh legs. But if I’m planning on going for a recovery run instead, there’s no need to change my plans. Should you ignore Garmin’s recovery time? I mean, there’s an argument for ignoring any metric a watch gives you, at least some of the time. You don’t need to let Garmin’s recovery time run your life. If you still want to get your workout in, and you feel up to it, feel free to ignore the recovery numbers.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
That said, I do find the recovery time useful as a gut check. If I get a long recovery time, that’s a reminder that I did actually work pretty hard, and I should make sure my efforts are balanced over time with easy and hard days. Any good training program will keep that in mind anyway—with or without a watch putting a number on it.Why does my recovery time keep changing?Garmin is constantly updating its estimate of how far away you are from full recovery. If you do another workout before the timer hits zero, the number will go up again because you’ve given yourself more work to recover from. On the flip side, if you got a good night’s sleep, you may find that the number shrank more than expected during the night. Again, you don’t want to read too much into this number; it’s just an estimate, after all. But it’s a good sign if you find you’re recovering quickly from your hard workouts.

title: I Let Claude Answer My Emails for Me, and Here's How It Went
description:
Claude's Gmail integration has gone up a notch.
                                                    Credit: Anthropic
body:
Claude's Gmail integration has gone up a notch.
                                                    Credit: Anthropic
                            
        
        If AI is going to take all of our jobs, the least it can do is make those jobs a little easier while we still have them, and email admin is one of the biggest time sinks I've got in my daily routine. I'm spending hours a week reading and responding to emails when I really need that time to get on with writing about new Pixels or Mac apps.My interest was piqued then by the news that the Claude AI chatbot can now respond to and send emails in a connected Gmail account–and without your specific approval, if you're happy to let it work automatically.Claude has been able to plug into Gmail accounts for a while, so you could already get it to read through and summarize incoming messages—but any email drafting had to be done in the Claude bot and copied over. Now the AI is able to compose and send responses inside Gmail without you having to switch over to the Google email client yourself.
Could this free up some more time in my day? Is it really wise to hand over emailing duties to an AI bot? I gave it a try to assess how it might impact my productivity (and sanity).How to connect Claude to your gmail accountYou need a paid Claude plan for this at the moment, so you're going to have to be on the $20-a-month Pro plan or something higher. To connect your Gmail account if you haven't already, open Claude on the web and click your profile picture (bottom left), then select Settings > Connectors and find Gmail. (If you don't see your profile picture, click the menu button, top left.)To do something in Gmail, you just need to mention it in a prompt. If you're not quite ready to do some drafting and sending, try a prompt like "who's emailed me most today" or "summarize the emails I've received this week." Claude rummages through your Gmail account and delivers what you asked for as a response.When you're ready to start sending, you can be pretty informal and ambiguous with your prompt. Saying "reply to my last unread email," "reply to David Nield," and "reply to the Story edits thread" will all work in Claude. However, the more precise you can be—with a specific email address, for instance—the better, in terms of avoiding mistakes.
    
            
            Gmail is one of many Connectors available in Claude.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
If you say "send an email to Dave" and Claude finds three people with that name, it will ask who you mean. However, if it finds the wrong Dave and misses the other two for whatever reason (maybe due to formatting or email address construction), it will make the incorrect pick and not tell you about it. So, be as precise as you can.Next, you tell Claude what to say: You can dictate the message word for word, or tell Claude to get creative and use its imagination, or do a mix of the two. This works the same as any other text prompt—supply as much or as little direction as you want regarding email content, style, intention, and other characteristics.You'll be relieved to hear that automatic sending is off by default. If you go back to Settings > Connectors, you can click Gmail to set permissions. Different actions, like searching through your inbox, sending emails, and editing labels, can be set to one of three different options: Never allow, always allow, or always ask for permission.Here's what happened when I let Claude manage my inboxI took the risk and gave Claude permission to send emails automatically without approving each draft and got to work. I did consider getting in touch with the Lifehacker editors, but keen to stay on the roster here and avoid any hallucinated misunderstandings, I decided to have an email conversation with myself, via a secondary email address.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Claude actually works really well for getting around your Gmail inbox: It understands labels, dates, contacts, subject headers, themes, and nuance. It easily identified "the email I've just sent myself from my Proton account" without me having to open up Gmail, and I told it to reply—saying that it should agree to a meeting and talk about the weather.
    
            
            Are you sure you want to do that, Dave?
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
One immediate problem: It signed off my email with "cheers,, something I would never say outside of specific scenarios involving bars and clinking glasses. I don't think I've ever used that in an email, but evidently a lot of people in Claude's training data have, which is why it was included. Be aware that Claude may not catch your default tone and personal nuances when you let it compose your messages.The rest of the email was fine, if a little generic: I agreed to a meeting (with myself), and mentioned the weather (a standard British conversation topic). I then repeated the process several times, giving Claude different levels of freedom when it came to composing message replies.On a technical level, it's all quite impressive. Claude can accurately pick up and transfer what's in an email thread and compose replies as instructed. I told it to generate a message summarizing my work for the week (via its Google Drive access), and to add a question about a weekend soccer match, and it did both with aplomb. We know AI makes mistakes, but I didn't see any in my testing.
    
            
            Claude does a good job at summarizing incoming emails.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
As clever as this is, though, the biggest issue is that I can't really see myself using it. To begin with, these emails aren't written in my voice or style, and I'd be continually worried that Claude was about to make a terrible error somewhere (maybe in misinterpreting an incoming email, or getting something wrong in an outgoing one).Another concern is where all this is heading: AIs emailing other AIs, into infinity? I already suspect a lot of the emails I get are crafted by chatbots, which immediately devalues them. If I'm going to communicate with someone, I feel I owe it to them to actually put together the message myself. While I think I'll keep Claude's Gmail connector around to search and summarize emails, the sending and drafting features are getting turned off for now.

Emily Long

After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C.             Credit: Herstockart via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're a Microsoft Edge user, you will soon find that some older extensions—like uBlock Origin—no longer work. That's because Microsoft is following Google Chrome's lead in transitioning to the Manifest V3 extensions platform and disabling MV2 add-ons in the process. Edge is built on Google's Chromium engine, so the change isn't unexpected, but it does impact users who rely on older ad blockers. Microsoft is ending support for older Edge extensionsMicrosoft recently announced that it will begin turning MV2 extensions off by default over the next few months, and support for these add-ons will end completely for most users by the close of 2026. (The transition for enterprise is expected to be finalized in early 2027.) Microsoft notes that 95% of MV2 extensions on Edge have already moved to MV3, leaving fewer than 60 in the Edge Add-on store still on MV2. That includes uBlock Origin, which does have an MV3 version in uBlock Origin Lite, but the latter isn't as powerful as its predecessor and hides content rather than keeping it from loading in the first place. AdBlock, AdBlock Plus, and AdGuard are other MV3 alternatives with Edge versions, though they are not perfect replacements for uBlock Origin either thanks to restrictions on how MV3 ad blockers are able to filter content. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you want to retain the ad-blocking features you're used to, you can move away from Edge (and Chrome) to a browser that's not Chromium-based. The alternatives also tend to be pretty decent when it comes to privacy. One is Firefox, which runs on its own Gecko engine and still allows these older ad-block extensions, including uBlock Origin. DuckDuckGo and Brave both have built-in ad-blocking capabilities. Note that Opera, which is Chromium-based, has said the platform plans to continue MV2 support for now, but that may end eventually.

title: 10 Hacks Every Facebook Marketplace Buyer and Seller Should Know
body:
Stephen Johnson
                            
        
            Stephen Johnson
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceStephen Johnson is a senior staff writer at Lifehacker covering pop culture and technology, including the columns “The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture” and “What People Are Getting Wrong This Week.”
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Image Credit: Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Through its focus on local selling, Facebook Marketplace has become the world's biggest digital garage sale, but without tables to browse and friendly small talk. Getting what you want, whether it's finding those low-priced gems or getting a good price for your old blender, comes down to understanding how both the platform and its users work. You can't treat it like an old-school classifieds page and hope for the best; you need tactics. Here are 10 strategic hacks to navigate the chaos, outsmart the feed, and get the best deals on both sides of the transaction.Download Google Lens, the most important app for both buyers and sellersWhether you're a buyer or a seller, you should download and use Google Lens. This scans a photograph, identifies the item pictured, and spits out all kinds of info about it, including prices from new and second-hand sales. It's an instant price-check that lets sellers know if their asking amount is in line with other sales, and it lets sellers know whether they're getting a good deal or not.  Here's a short step-by-step guide for using Google Lens on mobile:
Tap the Marketplace listing photo to open it full screen.Take a screenshot or save the photo to your camera roll.Open the Google app on your phone and tap the Camera/Lens icon located on the right side of the search bar.Select your screenshot from your photos.Lens will scan the item and pop up the exact product name, reviews, online retail pages, eBay sold listings, and more, so you know its real value before making an offer.Other apps that might be useful for sellers include Facebook's own Seller, an inventory management tool that organizes your listings and fully separates your Marketplace activity from your Facebook activity, and Crosslist, an app that lets you create one ad that can be posted on 11 different sites, from eBay to Poshmark. Change your location on Facebook Marketplace to find items for sale in more desirable areasMarketplace's focus on location-based sales makes it a mosaic of micro-economies instead of a unified market. Supply, demand, and seller desperation fluctuate wildly based on demographic and geographical lines, so expand your search beyond your zip code and target micro-markets. Here are some ideas:Wealthy suburbs: If you want high-end furniture, power tools, and designer clothing, target sellers in affluent neighborhoods who might value cleaning out their garage more than wringing every dollar out of a listing.College towns: The area around a university at the end of a semester can be a goldmine if you're looking for standing desks, computer monitors, and other student-y items. Kids with a hard move-out date and a plane ticket home will often sell their mini-fridges for almost nothing. City centers: Apartment dwellers moving between small spaces face strict lease dates and lack storage space, so urban cores are prime hunting grounds for lower-priced furniture, kitchen gadgets, and TV mounts.How to set up a targeted search:On desktop or mobile, click the Location filter at the top of your Marketplace feed (e.g., "Los Angeles, CA · Within 40 mi").Enter the specific ZIP code or town name of your target micro-market, rather than your home address.Shrink the radius slider down to 5 or 10 miles to isolate listings exclusively within that neighborhood.Include one honest flaw in your Marketplace product descriptionsIt seems almost counterintuitive, but when you're writing a product description, mentioning a flaw with a product you're selling on Marketplace can actually make it more desirable to buyers than saying it's pristine. Everyone is looking for an honest seller, and mentioning a missing knob on a stereo or a small scratch on a bookcase proves you're not trying to hide anything, and it makes people more prone to believe the good things you say about the product. It's a reassuring way of answering the unspoken question everyone has when buying: "What's wrong with it?"Game the Facebook Marketplace algorithm with a simple videoI'm shocked by how many people don't do this, but if you're a seller, you should include a video with every listing, even for things like sunglasses. First, because Marketplace's algorithm will place items with videos into more people's feeds. Secondly, it's "proof of life" and a reassurance that you're legit. Film the drawers sliding smoothly, the blender motor running, or a quick 360-degree walkaround in daylight and you've proven that the item exists, works, and matches your photos. Instant legitimacy. Use the "list in more places" feature to target niche groupsAfter you post a listing, tap the three dots on it and select "List in more places." Facebook will surface relevant Buy/Sell groups based on your item and location. A lot of sellers skip this step, but listing in these groups connects you with more people and a more informed community than a general ad. It doesn't cost anything, and it doesn't take long, so add your listing to every suggested group that's a reasonable fit.One thing to watch, though: Match your tone to the group. A post that reads fine as a standalone Marketplace listing can feel generic or spammy when dropped into a tight-knit local group.Know when to "re-list" vs. "renew" an adIf the ad you've posted doesn't sell and the views have slowed to a trickle, you have two options: renew or re-list. To deal with dead ads, Marketplace gives sellers a "renew" option for ads that have been up for seven days. The specifics of Marketplace's algorithm are secret, but insiders say that renewing only gives a brief, small boost to a listing. Deleting the ad entirely and putting up an identical one makes the item new again, but it should be done with caution. Facebook doesn't seem to like when users remove an item and replace it too often; it can even result in having your account flagged for suspicious activity. It also results in anyone looking at your profile seeing the same item listed and delisted, which is a red flag to many buyers. So you have to be patient. According to insiders, if you take down an ad and wait two months to re-list, it should show up as clean, but I can't say for sure, because the algorithm is mysterious. Follow this simple rule for Marketplace price negotiationsI can't stand haggling, but I've grown to accept that it must be done on Marketplace. A seller who states their price is firm will still be low-balled, and a buyer paying the sticker price is usually paying too much. You can get deep into the weeds when it comes to price negotiations, but for buying a second-hand sofa or something, it's easier to follow the 15% rule: If you're selling, tack on an extra 15% to be haggled away. If you're buying, offer 15% less than the listed price. Do this to be the first one to see new listings of items you really wantThis hack isn't for one-timers or occasional buyers and sellers, but if you're a hobbyist or collector, it's gold: When you've successfully purchased a Pokémon card or something from a seller you vibe with, give them your number and a friendly, "If you're selling any more Pikachus, send me a text. I'm always in the market." This can also work for parents of young kids who are buying hand-me-down clothing, toys, or electronics from other parents with older kids...those kids are going to keep outgrowing this year's jeans, and you can be the first one to put dibs on them.Dealing with a solid buyer saves sellers a lot of time weeding out flakes and low-ballers. As a buyer, getting a first look at coveted items gives you an advantage over the competition. And for sellers, it's easier dealing with someone you've already done business with before (and know they're going to show up to get the item when they say they will).Filter for $1 to find potential steals If you're new to Marketplace, you may be confused by the number of items listed for $1. People generally list for $1 for two reasons: to game the "sort by lowest price" algorithm to get their ad to the top of searches, or because they're selling multiple items with one ad. This is generally a bad strategy for sellers but can be great for buyers. I ignore the "gaming search results" group entirely—it feels dishonest, and the lack of a listed price gives you no starting point for a negotiation—but people listing a lot of things in one ad can lead to some great deals. Whether it's an estate sale, a yard sale, or a recording studio shutting down, some sellers post a single wide shot of a room full of stuff, set the price to $1, and spell out the specific contents and individual prices in the ad's description. Taking the time to click on these lot listings and reading through the inventory cuts out a ton of competition from would-be buyers who only search by keywords.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Use the two-hour test window to hack the algorithmAlways be around to answer questions for the first couple hours after you make a post on Marketplace. Marketplace shows new listings to a small test audience to see how many people click, save, or message, so the algorithm can determine how widely to push it. A lot more goes into how widely your ad is flung (price, desirability, etc.), but if you're there right after posting to provide engagement, it helps your ad be seen by a wider audience later on. Speaking of timing, there's a variety of opinions on when is the best time to post a listing, but there's no consensus. Some swear by 6–9 p.m., especially Thursday through Sunday, when people are off work and scrolling from the couch. Others point to weekday mornings, when there's a burst of activity as people ease into the workday. What you'll find for sale on Facebook MarketplaceNo hack in the world is going to help you sell something no one wants to buy, so I've put together a general hierarchy of what sells on Marketplace and what doesn't, in order of cheapest to most expensive.Furniture and heirlooms at bargain pricesThe greatest bargains on Marketplace are in heavy things with specific purposes. Above-ground pools, hot-tubs, pianos, and heavy china cabinets sell for fractions of their original price, and they're often marked down to "haul it away and you can have it" prices. Some unwanted items are amazing, too. A flagship console organ with double keyboards and foot pedals might have retailed for $20,000 in the 70s, but you can routinely find these 300-pound behemoths listed for $0 on Marketplace. If I had a barn, I'd get like seven of them and throw an amazing party. Here are other things sellers will struggle with but buyers can have for a song:Outdated, general interest technology: 720p LCD TVs, old wifi routers, and non-4K computer monitors are tough sales. New technology is just too inexpensive for many to want to step backwards. Particle board furniture: IKEA flatpack bookcases and couches aren't really meant to be transported and sold. Formal heirlooms: To our parents and grandparents, fine china, crystal stemware, silver-plated flatware, and porcelain figurines like Precious Moments or Hummel seemed like investments in the future, but it turns out the future doesn't host too many formal dinner parties, and your parents and grandparents probably didn't have good enough taste to collect rare, mid-century patterns that remain desirable. Hobby and sports items at low pricesThe next tier is the junkyard of failed hobbies, where sellers unload their old marching band saxophones, hand-me-down skateboards, entry-level bicycles, and rowing machines for "I just want this out of my garage" prices. So many bargains to be found for starting a new hobby. Mid-tier products for users who are trading up to the next levelThere are some categories that have a huge middle ground. Things like bicycles, audio equipment, and camera gear tend to have a large, dedicated core of users always trading up, so there's a lot of churn in the middle. Sellers tend to know what these things are worth, so you're more likely to find modest deals, but they're definitely cheaper than new. What you're unlikely to find: high-end, specialized gearHigh-end, specialized gear—commercial embroidery machines, boutique espresso set-ups, high-end woodworking machinery, etc—is rarely sold on Marketplace. These are often "keep until you're gone" items. Sellers tend to use non-local platforms to sell these, as the buyers are niche and know exactly what they want and what they want to pay.

title: You Can Have Google Meet Take Notes for Your In-Person Meetings Too
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 14, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Primakov/Shutterstock
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google Meet now supports notation for in-person meetings.
                                            Google is rolling out the feature to AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers, as well as compatible Workspace plans.
                                            If you have the feature, you can hit "Take Notes for me" in the Meet website or app to start note-taking for your conversation.
                                            You can also conference in someone via a Google Meet call and continue taking notes.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Google Meet's "Take Notes for me" feature is one particularly useful implementation of AI. When you're on a video call, Gemini can dictate what's being said, offering summaries and highlights of the conversation. Your attention doesn't need to be split between the conversation at hand and writing down notes to remember key points later: The notes are automatically generated as a Google Doc once the meeting is over. It's the kind of feature that sells me more on the whole "AI assistant" thing, much more so than an app trying to order me a coffee.     Video conferencing isn't the only time dictation can be useful, of course. An in-person meeting can benefit from the same perks as a virtual one: Why bother with scribbling down notes on paper or typing away on a laptop when your phone can transcribe the chat on your behalf? I've used the Voice Memos app on my iPhone for the task, since it's easy to record audio and an generate automatic transcription of the conversation that way. But if you're a regular Google Meet user, you now have a similar option in your app of choice, as Meet's "Take Notes for me" feature now supports live, in-person meetings too.  How "Take Notes for me" works in personAs noted by 9to5Google, here's how it works: You open the Google Meet site or app on your device, but rather than start a call, you can use the "Take Notes for me" option to task Gemini with transcribing and summarizing your discussion. You can hit "Pause" at any time to pause dictation, and "Stop" followed by "Stop taking notes" to end it altogether. You can also transition to a video call if you want to conference in someone who isn't in the same room as you. And, just as with a Google Meet call, Take Notes for me will automatically save the meeting notes in a Google Doc.
Google first announced this feature back in April, but is now widely rolling it out to AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers, as well as Workspace plans. If you have a Workspace account, your admin may need to activate it on their end, at which point you should be able to start recording your own conversations. Google says the feature works across platforms, but will roll out along different timelines: It has been trickling out to Android since Aug. 11; web users will start seeing it today, Aug. 14; and iOS users will see it starting Aug. 31.   
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Try an alternative to Google Meet's in-person dictationThere are plenty of alternatives if you don't have "Take Notes for me" available to you in Google Meet. It won't be a perfect match, since Google Meet integrates with your Google account and does more than just transcribe the call, but there are other options worth considering. As I mentioned, I really like using Apple's built-in tools: Voice Memos can generate automatic transcriptions, which you can save to Apple Notes. But if you don't have an Apple device or you prefer another option, PCMag has a series of recommendations, including Otter.ai, GoTranscript, and Rev.

title: Hackers Are Screen Sharing on Macs Without Permission, but You Can Stop Them
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 17, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: NguyenDucQuang via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Hackers are actively exploiting a known macOS security issue that lets them enable Screen Sharing without permission.
                                            Apple released three security updates for macOS that all patch the same serious security vulnerability.
                                            It's possible this flaw could let hackers not only see your Mac's screen, but also take over your computer entirely.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Whether you have a MacBook Neo or an iMac, stay vigilant: Hackers are exploiting a known security vulnerability in macOS that allows bad actors to activate Screen Sharing without the proper permissions. Because macOS lets screen sharers control screens remotely, this flaw is particularly dangerous. Luckily, Apple fixed this issue before anyone knew the flaw was exploited. The company released three new security updates for Macs on Thursday, Aug. 6. You don't need to be running the latest version, macOS 26, to take advantage of these updates, either. While the company does have a new Tahoe update, Apple's security updates here include releases for both macOS 15 Sequoia and macOS 14 Sonoma as well—and all of these updates patch this screen sharing flaw.Apple's latest macOS security patches fix a Screen Sharing vulnerability macOS Tahoe 26.6.1, macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, and macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 all contain the same, singular security patch: Tracked as CVE-2026-65400, this fix is for a Screen Sharing flaw that Apple says could allow an attacker on your network to "authenticate to Screen Sharing without valid credentials." In layman's terms, this security flaw could let hackers activate Screen Sharing without permission, which would leave the contents of your Mac's display totally open to anyone in the know.
Apple's Screen Sharing feature is complex, which is good for usability but potentially dangerous in this case. Not only can people using Screen Sharing see your Mac's display, they can, if prompted, take over your Mac as well. Typically, this requires permissions on both sides to activate, so a bad actor could also theoretically take control of your computer using this flaw—accessing your files, messages, or anything else on your Mac.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
At the time, Apple did not say that this flaw was previously publicly disclosed or being actively exploited, so it's not clear how long hackers have been using it. But it's likely we'll see more cases like this going forward: Certain AI models, like Claude Mythos, are adept at discovering security vulnerabilities, so it's possible someone out there could have found this flaw before Apple did. Luckily, the patch is now out for anyone running the latest three versions of macOS, so all you have to do to protect yourself is update your Mac.How to install this Screen Sharing security patch on Mac  Whether your Mac is brand new or a few versions behind, there's a very good chance you can install one of these security patches. To do so, open System Settings > General > Software Update, let macOS look for the update, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install it.

title: This Malware Can Take Over Web Browsers on macOS, but You Can Protect Yourself
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 17, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Perawit Boonchu / iStock via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Hackers are pushing an infostealing malware to macOS users that is capable of hijacking your sessions in Google Chrome and other browsers.
                                            AmnesiaStealer can copy a victim's Chromium profile, which allows it to collect data, access authenticated sessions, and control them remotely.
                                            The best way to protect yourself from AmnesiaStealer is to be vigilant against ClickFix attacks.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        In a new ClickFix attack iteration, hackers are pushing an infostealing malware to macOS users that is capable of hijacking your sessions in Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and a number of other Chromium-based browsers. AmnesiaStealer grants remote control of your browser and access to plenty of personal data, so you should know how to spot the campaign and protect your device from compromise. AmnesiaStealer hijacks your web browser on macOS As BleepingComputer reports, AmnesiaStealer can copy a victim's Chromium profile, which allows it to collect data across 16 Chromium-based web browsers, access authenticated sessions, and control them remotely. This means threat actors can navigate across websites, export or import cookies, and access online portals as well as grab saved logins, history, bookmarks, extensions, and cryptocurrency wallet data. AmnesiaStealer can also capture your macOS password and gain access to keychain data, Apple Notes, Telegram sessions, documents, and system information. Researchers at security company Jamf found that hackers are distributing the malware via a password-protected ZIP archive on a fake GitHub page and are gaining this level of access when users run a Terminal command that downloads and installs the payload. The campaign mirrors previously identified Atomic and MacSync infostealers. 
How to avoid browser takeover attemptsThe best way to protect yourself from AmnesiaStealer is to be vigilant against ClickFix attacks, which use social engineering tactics to deliver malware to your device. Common tricks include fake error messages, CAPTCHA forms, and, as in this case, command prompts that install malicious payloads that can then spy on your activity, steal your data, and take over your machine. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Threat actors count on you believing that these commands do something innocuous (like download legitimate software) or not understanding what you're executing on your device. That's why you should be highly skeptical of any prompts you find online and never execute commands in Terminal from non-official sources. Note that the fake GitHub page being used to distribute AmnesiaStealer has a "Verified Publisher" tag to gain user trust. Fraudsters will also try to impersonate legitimate companies—tech support scams are one example—so you should never copy and paste commands in your system dialogue even if you believe you're interacting with a trusted business or service.

Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.

        August 17, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Leon Neal/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            If you're struggling to access GitHub this morning, you aren't alone.
                                            GitHub appears to be down for users across the internet. Downdetector shows tens of thousands of user reports as of Monday morning.
                                            GitHub issued a fix at 12:36 p.m. ET, but says interruptions may continue as it rolls out.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're trying (and failing) to access GitHub Monday morning, you aren't alone. According to Downdetector, the hosting provider has over 15,000 user reports indicating issues or downtime with the service—up from roughly 3,000 reports when I first published this article. Whether you're a developer trying to update your repository, or you're a user trying to access one, GitHub may give you trouble. Luckily, the outages should be over soon. GitHub officially confirmed the outage through multiple updates to its status page. However, in the latest update at 12:36 p.m. ET, the company confirmed it fixed the issue: "We identified the problematic component and have taken corrective actions. There are strong signs of recovery but we are still working to completely restore service, with error rates still remaining slightly elevated. We will post further updates as recovery continues." As such, you might still see issues with GitHub as the fix rolls out. GitHub hasn't identified the exact issue yet. At 12:16 a.m. ET, GitHub posted an update that reads: "We are experiencing high error rates around 20% for web experiences and api traffic. Archive downloads and raw repository content downloads are experiencing an approximate 50% error rate. SAML and OIDC authentication, SCIM, and Team Sync are also impacted. We are still working to identify the root cause and will continue to post updates as we learn more and perform mitigation." 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If the comments on Downdetector are any indication, this is not the first time GitHub has had service issues. One comment reads: "Cmon [GitHub] get your sh*t together...this is getting old." (The user added their own asterisks.) Scrolling through the comment history, users reported errors one or twice a week throughout August. I'm not a regular GitHub user, so I can't attest personally to repeated downtimes, but it does seem as though this isn't wholly unusual. If you're still experiencing issues with GitHub, expect service to come back online shortly—assuming nothing catastrophic is happening behind the scenes.

title: Six New Features Coming to the Pixel Watch 5
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: René Ramos/CNET Group
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            The Pixel Watch 5 looks a lot like the Pixel Watch 4, but it comes with some exclusive new features and changes.
                                            The Pixel Watch 5 has an upgraded Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated chip that powers some of the company's on-device AI features.
                                            Google says the new watch has the most accurate GPS route tracking of any Pixel Watch, and beats the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        At first glance, you might think Google's new Pixel Watch 5 was actually the Pixel Watch 4. That's because it has the same "Actua 360 display" at an identical 320 PPI with up to 3,000 nits of brightness. And, just like the Pixel Watch 4, you can get the Pixel Watch 5 in either 41mm or 45mm models. If not for the new colors, you might think this year's watch is just like last year's watch. It doesn't help that many of the newest software features that Google announced along with the Pixel Watch 5 are compatible with older watches, too. Things like "Health Guardian," which tracks trends in insulin resistance, blood pressure, and sleep breathing, will be available on Pixel Watch 4 when they launch, just as they will be on Pixel Watch 5. But while the Pixel Watch 5 is a small update to the Pixel Watch 4, it is an update: There are six new features exclusive to the watch that you won't find on older models.  The Pixel Watch 5 comes with a new chipThe Pixel Watch 4 runs the Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 chip; the Pixel Watch 5 runs the Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated chip. That might not sound like a big difference, and, indeed, we don't have benchmarks at this time to say just how much faster the Pixel Watch 5 is than its predecessor. 
However, according to Google, the Pixel 5's "Accelerated" chip is powering on-device AI features faster than before. That includes Google's "Raise to Talk" feature, which lets you interact with Gemini by raising your wrist. The company says these features on Pixel Watch 5 now process "instantly with low latency," even when you aren't connected to the internet. The chip also powers Gemini Intelligence Proactive Suggestions (Google previously called this Magic Cue). These are new suggestions that automatically appear based on the context of what you're doing: If someone asks you for your flight info, Gemini can use your Pixel Watch 5's chip to dig through your apps to surface that info by presenting it as an option to share with a tap. Google says the Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated chip has 50% more RAM than the previous generation, as well as a 12% CPU boost, which makes the whole chip 20% faster overall.  The Pixel Watch 5 has highly accurate GPS route trackingGoogle has some bold claims for the Pixel Watch 5. Not only does the company claim that its newest watch has the most accurate GPS route tracking of any Pixel Watch (the company says it has double the accuracy of previous generations in the "toughest environments"), Google says its more accurate than Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro. We'll have to see how true those claims are when reviewers put the watch to the test.To make these leaps in GPS route tracking, Google says it tapped into Google Maps to "trace satellite ray paths through 3D building models." The company also explains how Pixel Watch 5 can connect to weather reference stations around the globe in real time to adjust for local atmospheric conditions. Google claims all these steps improve route precision.   
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The Pixel Watch 5 has improved sleep trackingWhile Pixel Watch 4 shares many of the new health features Google is rolling out in coming months, the Pixel Watch 5 does win in certain categories. Google says the newest watch has 15% more accurate sleep stage detection, which should improve sleep tracking overall. In addition, your bedtime automation on the Pixel Watch 5 can pause audiobooks automatically when you fall asleep, and there's now a dedicated bedtime watch face.New watch faces and complications on the Pixel Watch 5Google says Pixel Watch 5 comes with two new "stunning" watch faces, as well as 11 new "glanceable" complication styles. The company didn't highlight what those looked like in their press releases, but 9to5Google has images of the faces (Weave and Chronograph). You can also use AI to generate new watch faces if the available options aren't to your liking. Pixel Watch 5 comes in new colorsGoogle says the Watch 5 has three new color options, though only two are available in both sizes. Those include Fog, Olive, and Canyon, though the latter is a 41mm exclusive. If you're set on the 45mm model, you could instead choose the Stephen Curry Special Edition, as that model isn't available in 41mm.Breathing emergency detection (EU only)One health feature exclusive to Pixel Watch 5 is "breathing emergency detection." Google says the Pixel Watch 5 can use on-device AI to read its PPG, accelerometer, and barometer sensors all at once, in an effort to detect if you stop breathing. That could be from drug toxicity accidents, pneumonia, or choking. The company says if your watch detects a breathing emergency and you can't respond, it will reach out to emergency services on your behalf, even sharing your live location. This feature is launching in Europe first.
